title: The ocean rises
hook: three nights of asking, one burst of anger, and the ocean rises as a god with a nature of his own
carry: the elements are sacred, each with its nature

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, before a single stone. Rama awake on the shore at night, asking the wind to touch her, and your line, an avatar weeps, God took on a human heart.

Rama spreads kusha grass on the sand, the sharp ritual grass, and lies down on it, facing the sea. He folds his hands, asking the god of the ocean, Sagara, to show him a way across. One night passes. Nothing. Two nights. Three nights, fasting, waiting, and the water just keeps coming in and going out as if no one were there.
screen: `A BED OF KUSHA GRASS.` → `THREE NIGHTS OF ASKING.` → `NO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: On the fourth morning Rama gets up angry. Gentleness, he tells Lakshmana, is taken for weakness. He takes up his bow and fires into the sea. The waves heave, the sea creatures thrash, the water churns as if the end of the world had come. Lakshmana catches his brother's arm: enough. And Rama fits a terrible weapon to the bow, ready to dry the ocean to its floor. That's when the ocean rises. Sagara comes up out of the water in person, shining, garlanded, with the rivers around him, and speaks with folded hands. I can't change what I am. Earth, wind, sky, water, fire: each keeps its own nature, and mine is to be deep and hard to cross. I won't dry up. But if you build, I'll hold it up, and you already have the builder: Nala, son of Vishvakarma, the craftsman of the gods. Rama's arrow can't simply be put down, so he sends it north, and Valmiki says the land it struck became a desert. Now look at what just happened. The ocean is a god, with a voice and a nature of his own, and even Rama, Vishnu on earth, listens to him. Hindu tradition sees the whole world this way: earth, water, fire, air and space, the pancha bhuta, five elements, each with its own nature, each sacred. That's why Hindus bow to rivers, offer water to the rising sun, and call the earth Bhudevi, the goddess.
screen: `RAMA TAKES UP HIS BOW.` · `THE OCEAN RISES.` · `EACH KEEPS ITS OWN NATURE.` · `EVEN RAMA LISTENS.` · then, large: `THE FIVE ELEMENTS ARE SACRED.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus say a short prayer on waking, before their feet touch the ground. In English it runs: goddess, whose garment is the ocean, adorned with mountains, wife of Vishnu, I bow to you; forgive me for touching you with my feet. Then they touch the floor, and their forehead. Try it now: rest a hand on the floor. If you pray, say it in your own words. If you don't, simply notice the ground holding you up, and thank it.
The bridge. The ocean won't stop being deep, but it promises to hold up whatever is built, and it names Nala, Vishvakarma's son, as the builder.
Your line: the elements are sacred, each with its nature. Tomorrow, the building begins, stone by stone. Day six hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many Hindus say a morning prayer to the earth, Bhudevi, asking pardon for the touch of their feet before they step out of bed; at Rameswaram, the coastal town tradition links with this shore, pilgrims bathe in the sea.

kusha.meaning: a sharp grass used in Hindu ritual

Sagara.meaning: the ocean, and the god of the ocean

Nala.meaning: a monkey builder, son of Vishvakarma

pancha bhuta.meaning: the five elements: earth, water, fire, air, space

Bhudevi.meaning: the earth, honored as a goddess
